utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. Defence counsel, good morning. Mr. Vidovic, good morning to you, sir. Your Honours, it may just assist you in anticipating the progress of the morning, I think my conclusion of cross-examination will occur within the next 30 minutes. If that's of any assistance to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, the first yes question I do have to ask you as a matter of form, I think, is: Have you, at any time since the court finished yesterday, discussed your testimony with anybody at all?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I may go back to the times when you were awoken, because on the 20th of October, 1992 and again on the 16th of April, 1993, you say that you were awoken at 04.00 hours on both of those occasions. I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The first time, I think, was by Mr. Dragan Vidovic, the second time by Mr. Slavko Papic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we have heard from witnesses in this Chamber that a number of people, the first they knew, say, on the 16th of April, was that they were woken up by the firing, by the sound of explosions and gunfire, and is it true that that occurred something like an hour and a half after you were awoken that day?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Approximately at that time. Maybe a few minutes afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, we have heard here from a gentleman you know, Mr. Ivo Vidovic, that, for instance, as a village guard, he, in fact, was awakened only by gunfire on the morning of the 16th of April. So can you explain why you, as a village guard with limited involvement, were chosen to be awoken so much in advance of these actions on both occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why they woke me up and why they didn't wake up Ivo. I think that somebody woke up Dragan, they woke me up. We kept waking one another in turn, so it's possible that somebody came to Ivo's house later or perhaps he thought he wasn't woken up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the 20th of October you were, I think, aware, were you not, of roughly what the problem was because you had seen the barricades the previous day. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew, did you, that wherever any conflict may be it would be in the region of those barricades, if there was to be a conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you told us yesterday, sir, that on the 16th of April, however, you didn't know what was happening, you just thought there might be some trouble with the Muslims and you said you lacked information, you didn't know what was happening. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on that occasion, with no knowledge of the potential threat, you still performed the same actions as you had in October. You got up, you did not send your family to shelter, you simply went to the Sakic house, the same position as before. Now, can you comment, sir, as to why you took no precaution, say, for your family, when on that occasion you did not know what the threat was?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, precisely because I didn't know what the threat was I didn't take any stronger steps to move my family to Vitez or to another place, but at the time I didn't even know where it was, the safest place to put my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yet you say that, I believe, within a matter of metres of your own home, the Vrebac house, there was a strong shelter that was used that day by a number of other people. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. My family could have gone to that shelter in under a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the time when you were up near the depression in the ground, with the woods, and you say you mounted guard in those woods, or around near those woods with certain other persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Which conflict are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm talking exclusively now about the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: We were at Niko Sakic's house. Behind his house there is a barn and there's a little wood behind the barn, and then around that wood behind Niko's house towards Ahmici, we were standing there in groups of one or two. The rest were standing by Niko's house. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I got confused with this first and second, the 20th and the 16th of '93, the 20th of '92, because the same things were happening to me at that time. We, when the army had passed the people in camouflage uniforms, when the masked men, when they passed, after them Mirko, Zoran, Mica, I'm just speaking briefly because it's easier for me, we don't use our full names very often there. Dragan Vidovic, Dragan Samija went to the little valley beneath the Kupreskic house, to the left. You could see it, it was on the road near Sakic's house, near the barn. I went to Bijela Zemlja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that group of people went into this small vale or depression. I believe you described it previously as being surrounded by trees. So they were screened behind trees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: The depression is surrounded by trees and it's only three or four metres deep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you remind me, sir, as to what -- what did you understand the purpose of that group being in that depression? Were they on some form of guard? Were they setting up some kind of defence? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: They left to that depression just as I did, with the group of people in Bijela Zemlja to protect the shelters, the women and the children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in order to perform this protection, were this group armed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all armed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Some were. I had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm referring particularly to the group that went into the depression or small valley. You say they were armed as well?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, forgive me if I'm misunderstanding the situation, but if these people were being in a defensive situation, they were in a small piece of open ground, were they, in that depression and then surrounded by trees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I couldn't say that the area was open. It's protected by trees. It's a natural depression and you couldn't see it until you got to the very edge of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for defensive purposes, if they are inside the depression they would not see any enemy coming at them until that enemy had fully penetrated the trees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Practically, yes, unless somebody looked out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in fact, they were placing themselves, were they not, in a very dangerous position to be a defensive force, because their enemy would come upon them and be able to fire upon them from the cover of trees and they were in lower more open position? I could use the expression like rats in a barrel. They could be fired upon, could they not? Is that a good defensive position?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, it's not a good defensive position in my opinion, but those people were the not really knowledgeable about military strategy, so they simply placed themselves close to that shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge of those people, had any of them done their JNA service in the former Yugoslavia, their national service, had any of them done that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were all, to some extent, minimally trained, at least, as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, but it was a while since they had served their military term of duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this particular position I believe you confirmed yesterday that it was possible for people to leave that area and not to be seen by yourself because of the surrounding trees and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: From the place where I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you particularly stated that anyone going in the direction of the Kupreskic houses would not have been seen by yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I didn't say that. Anybody passing on the road from my house near Niko Sakic's house and going towards the Kupreskic houses I could have seen them, but from the depression itself, if somebody had left and come back, probably I wouldn't have seen them because I wouldn't probably have been looking in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they had gone from the depression onwards in the direction of the family Kupreskic houses, again you would not necessarily have seen them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't necessarily see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if, in fact, that group were just using that depression or clearing as a kind of holding area where they could come and going, but find some temporary safety during the day, they could have done so without your knowing necessarily; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: It's true, but I was -- I kept going to the depression. I went there three times, so I was there and I saw them every time that I went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On each occasion are you saying that each and every person who was initially in that depression was present, on each visit you made?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any occasions that you observed anybody, in fact, leaving that depression, perhaps going down to the shelters to visit their families near where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I could have seen it but I didn't. I didn't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just excuse me a moment, if you will, Your Honour. I think at that juncture I can conclude my cross-examination, Your Honours. So in fact I was 15 minutes adrift in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Blaxill. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac? Re-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic. You said -- would you please clarify for the Court one thing: How was it that in your shelter, in your house, the wife of Mirjan Kupreskic -- sorry; Zoran Kupreskic's wife, Mirjana, was brought, also Jasna Safradin was brought to your house? As you said, your family was there, and then refugees of the two Didak families came. Could you please tell us why these people came to your house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: The wife of Zoran Kupreskic came to my house with the children because I had directed them to come to my house. We're best men; we know one another well. His wife and my wife are good friends. Why did the Didaks come to my house? Probably because it was very crowded in the shelter at Vrebac. There were probably a lot of women and children, and the accommodation there wasn't the best possible. The house was close, it was very close to the real shelter. Jasna Safradin and her daughter were also there, across the street from my house. They were frequent guests. So ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they come there to seek shelter?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was your house treated as a safe place regardless of the fact that it didn't have a cellar?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your house well built, solidly built? Is it a new house, and old house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: My house is a new house. It's built from hard, solid material, from concrete. It has concrete columns, so it's very well built. It can resist shelling, even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people use to seek shelter in your house on other occasions before the conflict, between conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, they would seek shelter at my house later. When Buhine Kuce fell, other families would also come to my house, and they remained for a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your house was well built, and you took it to be a safe refuge?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes. It was away from the firing lines, about five -- 700 to 1.000 metres. It was sheltered somewhat by a couple of other houses, by trees, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What nationality were the -- were your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Generally they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said -- how many Muslim families were there close to you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: There was the Podojak family, the family of Ramo Bilic, his brother Zijad. They lived in one house, and one was living on the ground floor, the other was living on the first floor. And also their son-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the others were then of Croatian nationality?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described these events in the morning of the 16th, so it was the second conflict, or the start of the war in the Vitez valley; so could you please tell us -- you woke up at about 4.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, I was woken up at 4.00 a.m. I got dressed. At about 10 past 4.00 I left the house. I passed by my brother's house, which is in the same direction as Niko Sakic's house; it's about 20 or 30 metres away from my house. I tried to wake up my brother, but he wasn't home, so I started walking down the road. I met Anto Vidovic and Ivica Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were leaving, you were going towards the Sakic house, then you went to Niko Vidovic's house?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, I was there maybe at around 20 past 4.00 or 4.30; something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your neighbours were there, and then the neighbours of Niko Sakic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you saw Zoran and Mirjan with their families there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, at about 5.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I notice that this wasn't entered in the record yesterday: How many children did Zoran bring?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mirjan?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Mirjan also brought two children and his mother-in-law, who was ill. She was staying with them because -- she wasn't staying at her place, because she was alone there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he bring her?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: He was -- he put her in a cart, a wheelbarrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was taking her in the wheelbarrow?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they went in the direction of your house, and you also said that you talked to Zoran?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, I -- we stopped and talked, and I told him to take his family to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, the group of soldiers came that you've described. And which way did the group leave?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: They left on the road to the depression, towards the Kupreskic houses, towards the house of Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the direction of the Kupreskic houses?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a road there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Well, there isn't a real road; it's like a path. I used to go to school in Ahmici, so -- the road stopped at the Kupreskic house, but there is a path that led through the fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you saw -- after that you said that you saw Mirjan and Zoran coming back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, where did they go exactly, and who did they go with?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: They went to the depression with Mirko Sakic, Dragan Samir, Dragan Vidovic, to the depression, on the left side. When you enter there, you can enter straight ahead, but you can enter from the left or from the right. They entered from the left. They were just below the barn of Ivica's father, at the upper left part of the depression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when they left, was there already shooting then, or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: When they were leaving there was no shooting, but very shortly after that, the shooting started, and then we hurried as well. Somebody was missing something, Anto Brnada, but I waited for them. Their houses were right there across the street from Niko Sakic, so I stayed on the road at Niko Sakic's house, and then I saw Zoran when he was coming back again with Didak's family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he was coming back, you mean he was walking along the road towards your house again?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the road that leads to Santici?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the shooting started, when the first shots were heard, where were you, and what time was it then?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I was between the houses, on the road towards the position which I described in Bijela Zemlja. I'm not sure exactly what time it was, but it could have been 6.00 already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it have been earlier? Could you tell?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No, I can't really tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see Zoran when he came back from Santici, the second time, when he took the Didaks?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see the four of them in the first part -- Zoran, Mirjan, Vidovic, and Shamir -- could you see them in the depression, and as you described, could you see where they were positioning themselves beneath the barn?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, and I could see Sakic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next time that you came back -- you said you came back twice in the course of the morning?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes, at about 8.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find them in the same place in the depression where you saw them then?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the choice of the depression which the Prosecutor asked you about, do you know if the depression was used during the time of the JNA? Was it ever used during exercises as a natural shelter? Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the choice of your location and their location --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- was this exclusively your choice, or their choice?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody at any time say that they should take a different position, a better position, or that they should position themselves in a different way?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where -- what were the parts of the -- the outlying parts of the village that were being shot at? I'm talking about the part towards Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: The edges of the village were exactly along the road towards Ahmici from that other side, from the Kupreskic houses, up around the mosque. And then the lower parts of the village, also, you could hear shooting from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ever see Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic in uniform until the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they wear that day? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: Zoran had a jacket that was too big for him, because he is of slight build. He also had civilian clothes. He had shoes that were too big for him. Mirjan wore civilian clothes. I remember that he had white socks on, woollen socks. He wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the small problems we've had with the transcript, could you please tell us once again: When Zoran Kupreskic went down into the depression with Mirjan, after they came back, after what period of time did you see Zoran walk away with the Didaks?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: A few minutes later; two or three minutes later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say, immediately after they went down; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you see the Didaks? With Zoran, or did you see them before?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: With Zoran. When they were getting out of the depression I saw them. They passed by me all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Vidovic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. I have one or two questions. Mr. Vidovic, you may be of great assistance to the court by clarifying one or two points. Now, you said that on the 16th of April, '93 you were woken up at 4.00 a.m., by a colleague, a friend. I don't remember his name right now. Now, when you were woken up, did you ask why you were being woken up so early in the morning? Did you ask for the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I was woken up by Slavko Papic. He was banging at the door. I already mentioned that my bedroom was upstairs. I opened the window, since I was not dressed. I asked him, "What's up?" He said I should get up and go on guard duty because there should be quite a few of us who should be awake because possibly there could be problems. There could be a conflict, there is unrest, there was individual looting. Everybody would have to get up for the sake of their own safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that you spent about three days, I think, in that area on the 16th of April. So, 16th, 17th, 18th of April, if I understood you directly. Now, my question is whether you, say, on the 16th or 17th of April, whether you saw any Muslim troops or Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: No. No, I could not have either. From the place where I stood -- how should I put this? The river bank is on the opposite side from me, so I could not see Ahmici, and there are houses in front and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you -- did you notice at sometime, say, either on the 16th or 17th, any Croatian house being shelled, or destroyed or burnt down?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: I know that a few shells fell in the area of Zume, even in the field below my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean, did you notice, after the 16th of April, that any -- there was any Croatian house which had been, say, completely destroyed by shelling or, say, had been set afire?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN VIDOVIC (RESUMED)
utterances.text: A house in Vitez was burned down, Gavro Vidovic's house, and his sister's house was also destroyed in Gornji Pirici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you. I assume there's no objection to the witness being released. Mr. Vidovic, thank you for testifying in court. You may now be released. Thank you. (The witness withdrew) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, I presume? Good morning, Mr. Sakic. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself to the court?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: My name is Mirko Sakic. I was born on the 3rd of January, 1960 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live now? Could you tell us your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I reside in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about your education?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I am a technician in civil engineering. I'm involved in civil engineering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us what you did in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: In 1992 I was employed in the public utilities company Vitkom in Vitez. I was in charge of the construction operations, and I was in charge of a construction unit there. I did that for several years. Specifically in 1992, I was actively involved in several different construction sites that we had at that time inter alia. The last construction site I worked on was the Road of Salvation between Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did this? Who built this road?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: All the municipalities from Central Bosnia had their own parts. Zenica did one part, Novi Travnik did another part, Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca did a section jointly, fourteen and a half kilometres of that road namely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this road being built?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: This road was being built in mid 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why; since you're on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: This enclave was completely sealed off. The road towards Konira was cut open because the Serbs were there, and that was the only way supplies could reach the population. That's why it was called the Road of Salvation. After that I worked there for a certain period of time. The construction site closed down in the second half of 1992. I went on leave because there was hardly any work any more, and I started working in Horizont, a construction company from Vitez, and at that time, in the office of that company, there was the humanitarian organisation, the UNHCR it was called. This was in the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you start working for the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: No, not then. No. No, not then. I started working later for another -- another humanitarian organisation, ERCM (sic), an American humanitarian organisation that came in after the UNHCR, and I started working for them at the end of 1992 officially --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Sakic, you are speaking very fast. You really have to slow down, please. All right. Could you tell us now what is this organisation that you started working for, because the transcript isn't correct either.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I started working for an humanitarian organisation, an organisation called ERC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: National Rescue Committee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you worked for them until when?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I worked for them until the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live at that time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: At that time I lived in the village of Pirici. That is the local community of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point this out on the map, where your house was?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And tell me who your Muslim neighbours were, your closest neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: My closest Muslim neighbours were Sulejman Ahmic, who had a village house here, so to say. He lived in town otherwise. Then the Bilics, three Bilic families. One was abroad and two lived there. And then the Bilic's were here, I think. Here. Here. This is where they lived (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were your closest Croat neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: My closest Croat neighbours were here, Samija Nikola, Grgic Drago, Pudza and Kupreskic. Four houses of the Kupreskic family here. Over here. That's where they lived (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Please take a seat again. What was the name of this part of the village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The part that we lived in was called Zume, the lower part. Zume practically included -- I mean, part of two or three villages were called Zume altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Officially your village is Pirici; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Officially it is Pirici. And my house is practically 150 metres away from that border to Ahmici, so to speak, as the crow flies, and that is the barrier that divides these two villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take part in the village guards in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: At that time I did not take part in village guards in Pirici. That is to say that I had work duty, and at the beginning of these village guards, this was in 1992, the reason was immediate threat of war, war that was getting nearer and nearer, and these were people who were basically unemployed, because practically everything had ground to a halt. Later on I joined the village guard only once, I think, because the people who were there were complaining, and they said, "We were standing guard and you were not," and so that's why I decided to stand guard once. At that time I started doing this a bit. I can't remember exactly, but the Cheshire Regiment of the British army of UNPROFOR arrived, and since I had moved into Horizont I somehow managed to start working for them to do something, so I was kind of busy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a revolver and I had a hunting gun, and I had a permit, because after the fall of Jajce I bought an automatic rifle because there were weapons all over the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I did not go to the frontline. I never went to the frontline. As -- I never went there as a soldier but as a construction man, yes. Several times I went was Novi Travnik, Slatka Voda and Mravinjaci, where together with my construction unit I built fortifications, some small fortifications or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The positions that you mentioned, these were positions towards the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were positions against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the first conflict that occurred in Ahmici on the 20th of December (sic), 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I can give my own view of this conflict and the moment when I was there. As you know, the first conflict was on the 20th of October in 1992, and for me it started that morning, because before that I didn't know a thing about it. Afterwards I heard that there were some barricades on the road, and I came back from work late and I wasn't aware of this. On the morning of the 20th of October, around 4.30 in the morning, my father woke me up and he said that I should go downstairs. I went downstairs, and my children and my wife remained upstairs in the room. I thought that this was again one of the false alarms that had been happening for quite some time, because my house is the only one that has a basement there, and it was temporary shelter for all the neighbours when there was this kind of an alarm, you see. So I went downstairs and I wasn't really in a hurry. I thought that this was one of these many alarms, so I didn't take this very seriously, I must admit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you didn't know about the roadblock, that is to say that you didn't leave your home on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: On the 19th I was in Vitez, in the town of Vitez, all day. I came home in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you didn't see the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The roadblock is on the opposite side of the road that I had taken, so I did not really have a opportunity of seeing it. I just saw it only later, after the conflict that occurred there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened? You said your father woke you up?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, my father woke me up around 4.30, and I went downstairs and went in front of house. And in front of the house our neighbours had already started gathering, these are the Samijas, Nikola, Drago Grgic, Grgic's family, some of the Pudzas. They were there in front of the house. I got out perhaps 10 or 15 minutes after my father had awakened me. I went downstairs and these families were there, and we were talking. We were wondering what would happen. Truth to tell, we all thought that it was a false alarm. We spent some time there. Around 5.00 we heard some music and someone speaking from the mosque. I cannot identify it because -- because I didn't discern it. I didn't understand it. Immediately after that, perhaps a few seconds after that, I heard a double detonation, and then after that there was deadly silence, and my family went downstairs immediately. Everybody went down in the basement. We stood there in front, practically not knowing what was going on. We didn't even know what we were waiting for. We were waiting for something to happen, but I don't know. I don't know how to say this. We were, truth to tell, quite confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these families were going to the shelter, the neighbouring families?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the neighbouring families went to the shelter. We were standing in front there. We maybe remained there for an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we," you mean the men?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. So we were standing there in front. Then after a while, maybe at about 6.30, you could hear a lot of shooting from the direction of the cemetery. So the neighbours from Zume at that time came to us to see if we knew anything about what was going on. Zdravko Vrebac was there, Pero Jelic, Milutin Vidovic, Dragan Vidovic, and some others that I can't remember now. They came, and then somebody said, "Well, the Kupreskics are not here." We were standing close to my garage, next to my house, and then Zdravko Vrebac, and Milutin Vidovic, and Dragance Vidovic went towards the Kupreskic houses. Then a few minutes after that they came back with their families. Zoran, Mirjan were there, their wives, and the children. They went in the direction of Zume, and then later I heard, when they came back, that their children and their wives went to Zoran -- Zoran's and Mirjan's sister's house. Her name was Zorica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they come back?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course they came back. And we were all there, in the depression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did you position yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: We went to the depression between my house and the Kupreskic houses. It's a natural shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show us on the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. (Indicating). The depression is here. On all sides, it's surrounded by woods. There was a forest above that, but now that's been cut, so there is just some shrubs there now. During the former Yugoslavia, the depression was used as a place where all the citizens would gather in case of any kind of emergency, because it was safe from firing. It could not be penetrated by fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So what happened on that day? You were there, the neighbours were there; did you participate in anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely none of the neighbours. There was no shooting in this section. You could only hear shooting from the direction of the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see anything else? Were there burning houses? Could you see that anything else was happening in the village?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The shooting went on until the afternoon hours. During that time, the majority of the Muslim population from the lower part of Zume passed along the road. I can indicate it on the map. They went on the road towards upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, could you please show us the road.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Along this road. (Indicating). The population -- the entire population from here took this road. I don't know if it was everybody, but you could see this road from my house, so I could see that they were passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you see them passing? When was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I think that they started in the first half of the day. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was the Muslim population; that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they going?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I could see them passing along here. (Indicating). I couldn't see any further than that. There's a hill there, and then the road goes around, so that they probably passed that way, but I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After the shooting stopped, did the situation calm down in Ahmici? Did the Muslims come back?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The shooting stopped in the afternoon. Only after three or four days did people come back to their homes. The Kupreskics came back to their homes around that time, so at the same time that the Muslims came back, the Kupreskics came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they didn't return earlier?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, probably they were afraid; of course, they were afraid. We were all afraid of the possibility of the conflict's escalating and spreading to the rest of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any meetings being held in order to calm the situation down?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: A couple of days after the conflict, there was a meeting in the elementary school in Ahmici which was attended by the majority of the population there, mostly men, both from the Croats and the Muslims. And then there were Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak as representatives of the Croatian part of the municipality. I wasn't at the meeting, but my father told me, who attended the meeting, that they discussed ways to calm down the situation. So in order to prevent the escalation of the conflict which had happened near the cemetery. After that, I think even some decisions were made in order to compensate people for damage caused during the first conflict. One of the houses of Mehmed Ahmic Sudjuka burned, and then a few business facilities, I think: One that belonged to Miro Josip, and then a couple of other facilities. I don't know who the owners were. I didn't see any documents, but I heard that such a decision had been made, to help them with construction material in order for them to repair the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the purpose of the meeting in the school was to calm down the situation and to prevent escalation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The purpose of the meeting was primarily to prevent any kind of escalation and to try to restore the shaken confidence and trust. Then, as far as I know, it was also agreed at the meeting to try to establish joint village guards again. But I think that after that, a couple of days afterwards, this really stopped functioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what your father's name is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: My father's name is Mirko Sakic -- Niko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who took part in the meeting from the Muslim side? Who took part in the actions which were undertaken for the purpose of reconciliation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know, unfortunately. I think there were some leading people from the -- officials from the municipality, but there was a lot of people from the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much did the situation change in the relations between Muslims and Croats since the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Since the first conflict, many things happened. Three or four days after the conflict, Jajce fell, and then a large number of people came to Vitez. There were a lot of refugees. There was a lot of distrust; there was a lot of weapons. You could sense the insecurity. The majority of the Croats from Jajce continued on towards Tomislavgrad; a very small number remained in Busovaca. A part of the Muslims also continued on towards Zenica, and some remained in Vitez and in the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there, at the end of '92 and '93, and between those two conflicts, were there any occasions where there was a kind of emergency among the population? Were there situations when Muslims or Croats had to flee their villages, go to some other houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were constant alerts. This atmosphere was charged with insecurity. Every day you could hear detonations from the direction of Travnik. People constantly were coming from the front lines. Muslims were going to the front lines towards Kercici (phoen). They had regular shifts. All the people used to come and they would bring different information, so there was a lot of insecurity. There were false alarms quite often, when -- this happened at least four or five times, probably even more than that, when people would come to the shelter at my house expecting that something will happen, an attack, which never materialised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you worked for the IRC, the International Rescue Committee, the international organisation which had headquarters in Vitez at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. At the time -- so on the 15th of February, I had officially started to work. I was accredited to work for the IRC. I was an engineer in the field; I travelled. At the time, the organisation, the IRC, and I went together with them to Trnovo. This is a town towards Gorazde. And we formed a refugee camp there called Grebak, which was 20 kilometres away from Gorazde. Then in Vitez, the company that I worked for would make housing for the refugee camp. So we would assemble these housing units in the refugee camp. After that, we built six more such facilities, which were very easy and quick to build, and they were very easy to transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you if the IRC, before the first conflict, moved from Vitez, and where did it go?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the year, the UNHCR had moved to Zenica, because it had a lot of new people coming in, a lot of new staff. So they moved to Zenica because they needed more space. But the IRC remained. IRC moved from Vitez to Zenica on the 15th of March, and they did it quite hastily. I know this because a friend of mine who was working there was trying to reserve space in the kindergarten in Zenica. And then after that, everybody left for Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the departure of the IRC influenced by the bad security situation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. I remained as an associate of theirs in Vitez, and then after that I went to Gorazde together with them. Once more, I don't know why they left. I don't know the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing before the second conflict, so on the 15th of April,'93?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Two or three days before the second conflict, we had just completed the construction of some housing units that I mentioned, the six housing units, and they were loaded on to IRC trucks in Vitez. Then for Friday morning at 6.30, I was supposed to be at Kaonik, and I was supposed to go to Trnovo. On Thursday I went to work. I worked late, maybe until 7.00, 6.00 or 7.00 in the evening. I came back home, and I meant to get ready to go to Grebak the next day. My father told me that the family of Ivica Kupreskic had just come back from Germany, so since they were away, Ivica's wife had been away as a refugee for a year in Germany. A few days before that his children had come back. So I went to see them; they're close neighbours of mine. I went to see them at around 8.00 in the evening, to see them, to have a little chat with them, because there were stories going around that you couldn't go in or go out of the valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show where Ivica Kupreskic's house is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other houses are there besides his one?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: This is Ivica Kupreskic's house; this is his brother Josip's house; then Branko Kupreskic's house. This is the old house of -- Ivo Kupreskic house. There are a few farm buildings here, then Zoran Kupreskic's house is here, and then this is Mirjan and Anto Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that part -- that is where there were exclusively homes belonging to the Kupreskic family?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can sit down. So you went to visit Ivica Kupreskic; what relation is Ivica Kupreskic to Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: They are cousins. We got there, we were in the basement of his house. There were a few of us there: Ivica Kupreskic, there was his wife, I was there, Mirjan was there, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Miroslav Pudza; I think that the late Miro Vidovic was also there. So there were a few neighbours there. Ivica's wife had brought something for us to drink, and we were drinking, and then at about 10.00 I said, "I have to leave early in the morning to Trnovo," so I left. I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you talk about? What were the news that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: That day, Zivko Totic was captured in Zenica and four members of his escort were killed. So I heard that while I was in Vitez in the afternoon. And we were commenting, discussing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, we also discussed ordinary, everyday things, how their trip was. This was what we were interested in the most, because I didn't know what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't know what the situation was on the road. You were interested in if they were passable?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what we were really interested in, because there was talk that you couldn't pass at all. So Ivica managed to pass in a way known only to him, so this is what we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you went home in order to prepare, because you were going to Grebak the next day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I went home, I went to sleep. I simply went home. My father woke me up again at around 4.30, and again he said there'll be some kind of alert. I didn't really take this seriously, because these false alerts were continually happening. So I went outside in front of the house. The neighbours were gathering there already in front of the house. These were the Samija family, Nikolic Drago's family, then my father's family. I didn't even call my wife and my children to come downstairs. They were still asleep. Then there were neighbours. Miroslav Pudza was there. Other neighbours were gathering in front of the house. All of the closest neighbours who usually would collect in front of the house. So we were standing in front of the house just talking back and forth, "This is probably just another false alarm." We remained there for some time, and then the family of Dragan Vidovic came, and also the family of Stipan. His father, his family too came to the shelter. Then around that time, at maybe 5.00 a.m., Zoran Kupreskic passed along the road with three children and his wife, Mira Kupreskic, and right behind him there was Mirjan Kupreskic who was -- who was pushing his mother-in-law, his wife's mother, in a wheelbarrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was he pushing her in a wheelbarrow? What was wrong with her?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: She was paralysed. She was living with them at the time. She was paralysed. And she was holding a bag in her lap. His wife, Ljubica, and two children was walking behind them. She was carrying one child and the other child was walking, and they went in the direction of Zume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in your house at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: All the families that I mentioned stayed in my house, the family of late Drago Grgic, Nikola Samija, the family of Stipan Vidovic, the family of Dragan Vidovic, my brother's family, my wife, my mother. So all the people who were in the neighbouring houses, they all stayed at my house. Shortly after Zoran and Mirjan had left in the direction of Zume, maybe five or ten minutes after that a group of about 25 or 30 armed men appeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you standing then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: We were -- we were --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we could stop here because this will go on for some time. So we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, may we go on? You said a group of 25 to 30 armed soldiers came.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The group of armed soldiers in full military equipment came by. They had camouflage uniforms, some were wearing black uniforms. They were fully armed with automatic weapons. Most of them were carrying the RPGs, rocket launchers. Some of their faces were covered with paint, dark paint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I recognised one man who was a large man. That was his characteristic. That was Mirjan Santic. I recognised him because he's a very large man. His face was not covered with paint. There was an unusual detail that I noticed about him. It was a blue scarf that he was wearing around his neck. That's how I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you conclude on any basis which unit these people belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult to tell what unit they belonged to, but a few of them had white belts, so I could only assume that that could have been the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which way did they pass? Could you please show us on the map? Which way did they come?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: They came from the direction of Zume. That is to say, this way (indicating). At the point when I saw them, I was here (indicating). So that was the group of people who were there. So that is where we were, in front of my house. Then we went behind my house, and there is a farm building there and a garage, and we went towards the Kupreskic houses, this way (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who went there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: This unit that had come went towards the Kupreskic houses, through this part, this depression (Indicating). What should I call it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you see them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, from the place where we were, that is this garage of mine, we could see them up to here approximately, and then they moved towards the slope there (indicating). So we couldn't see them after that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you see any other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: No, no other soldiers. I didn't see any soldiers over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As they moved towards these houses that you called the Kupreskic houses, or in that direction -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you? What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: We stayed there by my garage, and we could partly see that part of the road, for a few minutes, five or ten, I cannot exactly remember. After that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic came and they joined us -- joined this group of people who were there from this valley, from this other part, from this other direction, from the Kupreskic houses. How should I put this? Two women with children were walking down. They were refugees. I didn't know them. They had arrived there only recently and settled down in Branko Kupreskic's house, and they asked Zoran Kupreskic where he had taken his wife and children. He told them. Because they did not know where this was, he took them again in the direction of Zume. Mirjan Kupreskic, at that time, was there with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after that? Did you stay by the garage or did you move from there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: We only went down into this depression below my garage. My garage is about 20 metres away from the depression that I mentioned in my earlier remarks. We went down towards this depression and that is where we stayed. That is approximately a few minutes after we went down into this depression. It could have been about 5.30. And from several directions we heard terrible small-arms fire. As soon as the shooting started, Zoran Kupreskic went back, because he had seen his wife (sic) off only partly. And he ran off. I remember that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. The translation is not right. Who did he see off partly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: His -- the family Didak. He saw them off. I didn't know them then. I think they still live up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So he came a few minutes after the shooting started, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as the shooting started practically, he came from the direction of Zume and joined us in this depression where we were all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show on the big map the actual place where this depression is? Where is this in the forest that is by your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The depression is here (indicating). The forest is here, tall trees, and there is a path, a pedestrian path leading to the Kupreskic houses. And we encountered this family over here, somewhere by my garage (indicating). That is to say, from the garage to here is about 20 metres. Then this is where the depression starts, and then the depression is approximately in this part over here (indicating). That is practically this entire area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is the area in which you were at the point when the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the area where we all were, all of us whom I mentioned before. So that was at the point when the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly who went into this depression? Tell us who was there when Zoran returned, and then you went, and you also said that Mirjan was with you. Who else?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: In the depression, at that time, I was there; Mirjan Kupreskic was there; Drago Samija, one of our neighbours, that is. Then -- then Drago Grgic; then there was -- I think, Dragance Vidovic was there too. Then I think -- it's difficult for me to remember now really all the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please sit down again? Thank you. In addition to this shooting that you heard from several directions, was anything else going on near this depression?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: All of us were there. All of us happened to be there, and Zoran came and said, "My parents went by," and he said, "They practically didn't help me and my wife at all to take the children. They ran away on their own because they were terrified." That is a characteristic detail that I remember vividly. We went up to the depression, to the top of the depression by the Kupreskic houses, and at that moment near us, in another small depression, a small mortar shell fell in there, and we had no war experience whatsoever, and it fell very close to us and we froze. For quite some time we did not move for a millimetre. We didn't dare breathe. How should I put this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us why -- why did you go to this depression? What was the reason why you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: As I said a few minutes ago, the depression itself is natural shelter, and since all our families were -- I mean, at my house there were already so many families, and then there were so many other families that could not fine a place to stay, and we simply reacted in the customary way. We had to be nearby. We didn't know what was going on. Our families are there, there's shooting. We were confused, we didn't have any information. I should say that they did this instinctively. We lived there. This is 30, or 40 or 50 metres away from my house. It was only logical to stay in that depression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see from that depression what was going on in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: As I said, we could hear shooting from several directions. From the Kupreskic houses we could hear strong small-arms fire, and also from the cemetery we could hear strong small-arms fire, and also from the direction of the elementary school we could hear strong small-arms fire. From that place, the place where we were, we were naturally protected there, and we were quite lower than the rest of the terrain over there. About 15 minutes afterward, we saw the first smoke that was coming up from the direction of the Kupreskic houses. During the day the smoke spread and we saw it in Donja Zume later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the houses that were on fire or did you only see the smoke?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: From the place where we were, we could not see which houses were on fire. However, the smoke was very strong, and over there it was the smoke from the direction of the Kupreskic houses. At that time I could not see. Absolutely no one could see the houses from there. We could only judge by the direction that it must have been those houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to give these photo files to the court and the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D85/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, could you tell us what is depicted in these pictures? What can we see on these pictures?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: On the photograph that I'm looking at right now is the depression that we were at during those moments we mentioned a few minutes ago. And it goes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the houses that we can see on the photograph, number 1?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: This is the house of Drago Grgic and Nikola Omazic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show us on the big map, on the big aerial photograph, where these houses are, the ones that you can see on photographs 1, 2, and 3 respectively?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: It is the houses over here that are at the very edge of the depression that we were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say that these photographs were taken --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: These photographs were taken from this direction; that is to say, from the Kupreskic houses, and moving towards Ivo Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. These are the houses that are at Zume; is that right? Lower at Zume; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at the other photographs. Photograph 4: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph 4 was also taken from the direction of the Kupreskic houses, but along a different path. It shows the road towards Pirici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does Photograph 5 also depict this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph 5 also depicts this, but from a different angle, from the direction of my house, or rather my garage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you just show us on the big photograph, which is the part of Zume that we can see on these two photographs, 4 and 5?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: On photograph 4, it is this part. (Indicating) It is this part that we can see, and on photograph 5, we can also see this part (indicating), but from a different angle. So it is this part up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is actually on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the right-hand side when we look from the direction of the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photographs 6 and 7? Or rather photograph 6; let's have a look at 6.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph 6 was also taken from the direction of my house, towards Pirici and towards the beginning of the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say that it is further off to the right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, further off to the right, towards here, moving towards here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph 7?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph 7 -- photograph 7 was taken from the exit out of the old mine directly towards the Kupreskic houses. So the photograph was taken from here (indicating) towards here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The houses that you can see, which houses are they? Could you tell us that? These are the houses on photographs 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: On photograph 7, we can see part of the farm building that is the one owned by Ivo Kupreskic. And the other building was not there at the time of the conflict; it was built later. I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What building? The first one, that you can see a bit more?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The one that you can see less is the one that existed before. And this one here that I'm showing now (indicating) was built subsequently, after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other building is a farm building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a farm building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the place where you were, could you see this building that did exist at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: We could only see the upper part of it; that is to say, part of the roof. Not even the entire roof, but part of the roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, please, could you take a look at photographs 9 and 10 as well.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph number 9 was taken from the depression from Ahmici in the direction of the lower part of the Kupreskic houses; that is to say that this is this natural depression, and it also depicts a forest in the direction of the lower part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us this on the map?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: It was taken from down here, from the depression, towards here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph 10?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph -- Photograph 10 shows from another angle -- it's a similar photograph. That is a photograph that was taken from here (indicating) towards here; that is to say towards my garage, along this line over here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And photograph 11?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph 11 shows fully the path leading to my house and my garage, so it was taken from here to here, exactly leading to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say the path along which you had left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first building we can see here is your garage; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photographs 12 and 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph 12: This could be this forest here. This forest over here (Indicating). And I think that the photograph was taken from the forest, as if it was taken here, by this edge, as if one went up here (Indicating) by the edge and then took a picture of the forest from this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see a house back there; can you tell us which house this is? Because this was taken from the direction of the Kupreskic houses; you can see this from photograph 8, and has a little cross there which shows the place where these pictures were taken from.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what direction this was taken from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the direction of the Kupreskic houses, towards your houses. There was a circle that was made. Could you tell us ...

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: It is really very hard for me to tell. I cannot -- I cannot tell for sure. No, no, I can't really tell. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could this be the house of Rudo Vidovic, the one that you can see in this direction?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, then, this was taken practically through the forest, and possibly -- yes, possibly this may be Rudo Vidovic's house. There would have to be another depression here in front, and then only Rudo Vidovic's house on the edge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel, may I ask you when these photographs were taken?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This year. In January, 1993 -- I'm sorry: '99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. So I imagine in April '93, it was totally different; I mean, there was no snow, probably, and the trees were different.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes. It is not quite certain as far as the snow is concerned in that part of Bosnia; it is possible that there could have been some snow even then, but not much of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Sakic, whether there were more leaves at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: On that day the weather was pretty bad, and I think that the leaves were not fully developed yet; they were just budding, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the exception of this one building that was built on the side of the Kupreskic houses, has the situation changed at all in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nothing else has changed, except for the forest, that was practically cut down completely. The rest must have been the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is to say that the forest is not as thick?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go from that depression, and when did you go from that depression?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: We remained in the depression for a while, and then between 9.00 and 10.00, Zoran and I went to see how our families were doing. We stopped by at my house first. We went to the cellar; I saw my family, and then the other families that I mentioned earlier. Then we went in the direction of Zume. Zoran, Mirjan and I went in the direction of Zume to see where their families were, how they were settled. One of the families was in the house of Milutin Vidovic and the other family was in the house of the sister of Zdravko Vrebac. We went there, and then a little bit before we came to the houses, we met Anto Vidovic, called Satko, who told us that one of our acquaintances, Fahran Ahmic, had been killed. Satko was very upset, and Mica -- Mirjan Kupreskic literally started to cry, because they played in the band together, and they were practically inseparable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did Satko know that? Did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Satko told us that Fahran's mother -- we called her Hasimovica -- that she was in one of the Vidovic houses, that she had gotten there from her house. So that's how he found out and then told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: After that, we went to the house of Milutin Vidovic; then we went to the shelter of Zdravko Vrebac. We stayed there for a short time. And we were quite shaken up by that news. We came back to my house. It could already have been around 11.30 or -- 10.30 or 11.00; I don't know exactly. So we met Nikola Omazic by the garage, the neighbour. He was a little -- he was slightly drunk, and he told us that Mirjan Santic had been killed in the direction of the Kupreskic houses, and that he needed to go there. We asked him where, and he said somewhere around -- close to the house of Ivo Kupreskic, or thereabouts. So then we passed through the depression, and then we reached the upper edge of the depression. Myself, Mirjan Kupreskic, Dragan Kupreskic, Zoran Kupreskic, Stipan Vidovic; I think Dragance Vidovic was also there. We went there, and then Nikola crawled up, and he reached Ivo's house, and then Ivica Kupreskic, and he brought Mirjan Santic's body -- they used a ladder; they brought the body to where we were.
