And then Dragan Vidovic, Stipan Vidovic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Zoran Kupreskic, and Nikola Omazic placed him on a ladder and they took him to my garage. We stayed around the garage for a while, and then his father came, and some relatives from the direction of Santici. And then they took him, took the body with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Mirjan Santic that you mentioned, was he a member of the military police? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Mirjan Santic? Well, it's possible that he was a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Mirjan Santic was wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any markings indicating to which unit he belonged on that uniform, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. They all had light bands on their shoulder. But I was in such a state that I wasn't really curious; I didn't look. The only thing -- and I mentioned this before -- a few of them were wearing white belts. This was characteristic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D86/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, would you please look at this document. It's an extract from the registrar of deaths for Mirjan Santic. Place of death is Santici; place of residence, Vitez Santici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date of death is the 17th of April, 1993; is that correct? Or is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: That is wrong. Mirjan Santic was killed on the first day exactly of the conflict, at the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mirjan Santic lived in Santici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he lived about 1,5 kilometres or 2 kilometres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at this photograph; it's on page 3. Is this person in the second row, the first photograph in the second row, is that Mirjan Santic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mirjan Santic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says there that he was born on the 5th of June in 1956 in Vitez that he's married, has two children, and that he was in the military police from the 16th of January in '93 and that he was killed on the 16th of April in '93 in Vitez. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So regarding the place of death, you know that he was killed at the Kupreskic houses?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was killed there, for sure, and a lot of people can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to explain something: This photograph and these six photographs that are on the second page of this document are photographs -- they were copied from this book, the book is called "Three Years of Military Police." I will use a few photographs from that book today, and also some of the text from the book. The Prosecutor is familiar with that document, because they used extracts from the book in the Blaskic case. I can provide the photographs for you to look at, to see, to make -- so you can see that this photograph is in the book and the text that I will be using are in the book. I don't have the originals, but I have translations of the text that I will be using. I also want to say that parts of the book were used in the Blaskic case as Prosecution evidence P457, and they were admitted into evidence. Now that we're talking about the book, you mentioned Mirjan Santic. Could you please tell us if you know whether anybody else other than Mirjan Santic was killed in Ahmici on that day, among the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I know that Zlatko Ivankovic was killed on the Croat side. I knew him well personally. He used to work in my company through the Youth Alliance, and his father was a foreman in my company. His friend was also killed, Zepackic. They were killed together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned Zlatko Ivankovic -- could the usher please take these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D87/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is also a death certificate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the death certificate for Zlatko Ivankovic. The day, the month and the year of death are the 16th of April, 1993, place of death Ahmici. Could you please look at page 3? The photograph in the middle of the first row, is that Zlatko Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Zlatko Ivankovic, son of Ilija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you heard from his father; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard from his father maybe a couple of days after it happened. It is also stated in this document, on page 3, that he was a member of the military police from the 3rd of January, '93, and that he was killed on the 16th of April, 1993 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the photograph is also taken from the book "Three years of the military police," that I showed earlier. You said that he was killed with another person; they were killed together. What was the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I heard later that he -- that that was Zepackic. I don't know the first name. His last name is Zepackic. They practically died at the same instant somewhere close to the Catholic cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you found that out later?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would the usher please take these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D88/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This another death certificate. The name of the person is Ivica Zepackic. He was killed on the 16th of April, 1993. He was -- also on the 3rd page, there is a photograph of Ivica Zepackic. Do you recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him, so I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is stated here that he was in the military police from April 28, 1992, and that on the 16th of April, 1993 that he was killed in Vitez. Did you hear that any other members -- I mean, any other Croats were killed in Ahmici on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard two other names later. I didn't know the people. A man called Arapovic, I think he was probably from Busovaca, and also a man called Rajkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you hear about that, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I think a few days after the conflict broke out, maybe the fourth day, when I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the usher please take these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D89/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a person called Arapovic, from Busovaca, was killed. Is it possible that this is Zeljko Arapovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that that person had a nickname perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I heard about somebody who was called Tata. I don't know whether that was Arapovic or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Zeljko Arapovic, born in Busovaca in 1962, and was in the military police from May 1, 1992, and he was killed on the 16th of April in Vitez. There's one more document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D90/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you had heard that a person called Rajkovic was also killed. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a picture of Slavko Rajkovic. He was in the military police from the 20th of November, 1992, and he was killed on the 16th of April, 1993 in Vitez. So these are photographers from the book "Three Years of the Military Police." The book was issued by the Defence Ministry of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in April 1995. Just one more thing in relation to the military police. You said that you had assumed that the policemen -- sorry, that the soldiers who passed in the direction of the Kupreskic houses were members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I said that for the following reason: A few of them had characteristic white belts, leather belts with holsters, and the members of that unit used to wear them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the military police was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of the name Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but much later, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to show this text.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D91/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a text that was written by Pasko Ljubicic, and that was published in this book entitled "Three Years of the Military Police." It was called both a combat unit and the police, and in the text it says the following: "When I mentioned the activities and tasks of the military police, this is my personal opinion, but I believe the military police in Central Bosnia is the most organised force in the defence of these territories which sacrificed a great deal, and at certain points in time it was of decisive importance in the defence of these areas." And further on it says: "I can mention Grbavica in this context, Sivrino Selo, Zabrdje, Kruscica, Ahmici and several other places, which I'm sure, and can prove that they were successfully protected -- successfully protected through the involvement of the military police." In view of what you said, and in view of the fact that the commander of the military police at that time claimed that he was there, can you conclude that the military police took part in the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: As I said a short while ago, the unit that was coming in our direction from the direction of Zume, as they passed by us some of its members had white belts and holsters. Since this is characteristic of the military police, it is logical that I thought this was a military police unit or part of a military police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to put you in a position to say that it is only the military police that attacked someone, that's not what you're here for, but you just tell me the following thing: Did you see the member of any unit on that day in Ahmici, or, rather, in the part of the village that you were?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: In the part of the village that I was in, I saw only this unit that passed by us, and I absolutely did not see any other unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now we shall go back to the events of the 16th. So Mirjan Santic was staying at the shed that belonged to your father's house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was brought there, as I mentioned a few minutes ago, and that's where we all were. His father came and they carried his body in the direction of Santici. I mentioned that his house is about a kilometre and a half away from my house, as the crow flies, and that's where they took him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His father came to collect him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. His father and probably there was someone else there, but I really cannot recall. They went there and we stayed here, and there was constant shooting, and most of the shooting could be heard from the direction of the mosque and the cemetery. It seemed constant from that direction, from the upper part of the Kupreskic houses. It seemed that it was moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say towards where?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Towards the village. Towards the middle of the village of Ahmici. That was around 11.00 or 12.00, I don't know, noon. And we could also hear the English tanks and APCs that were passing along the road, and they came to some parts of the village, namely to Zume, and they went back. At the moments when they were there, when we could hear them, because they were very noisy, then the shooting would subside a bit. Then it would continue with even greater intensity when they would leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you think? What was going on in Ahmici? You said that you saw smoke coming from that part of the village, from Ahmici and from Zume, in the afternoon; is that correct? What did you think? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: As soon as we saw smoke, we realised that something dangerous was going on. Indeed, we had not been informed about anything. We were taken by surprise. We were at a loss in terms of these events and this place. We were there, we lived there, our families were there. To say that I was confused would be putting it mildly. I was horrified. It is only then that I became aware of the fact that this thunder that could be heard from afar earlier on came right to us. I often say that this was the instinct of a herd that led us to gather there. We wanted to protect our own folk. We did not have any information. I was running about. The phones were dead, so I was calling people we knew from other parts of town. There was shooting over there too, and no one practically had any information that would have been sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people move out of your shelter, that is to say, your family and the people who were in your house, and why?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Since the shooting did not subside and bullets from small arms were coming to my house constantly, and in view of our lack of experience, it seemed to us this was terribly close. All these families ran away from my house, about 200 metres away from my house into a shelter that we thought was safer, and that was the house of Niko Vidovic. In the late afternoon, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your family also leave?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: My family also left, my wife and two children and these three or four families that were in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show us on the aerial image where this shelter was, Niko Vidovic's, that is?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: From the shelter at my house, the women and children went along this path, and this is where the house and basement of Niko Vidovic are (indicating). So that's where they came to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us Milutin Vidovic's house, and also the shelter where Zoran's wife was?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Going further along the road we came to this crossroads, and this is where Milutin Vidovic's house is (indicating), and down here is Zdravko Vrebac's house and also his sister's house (indicating). That's where the other shelter was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these houses of Jozo Vrebac and in this house where -- where Milutin Vidovic was, were there any other civilians there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: There were many civilians, many women, children, the elderly, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can sit down now. Your house has a basement; doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it had been treated as a shelter earlier on too?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: It was treated as a shelter as soon as the air raids began, and the families from the neighbourhood sought shelter there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say that every time it served its purpose well. What was the main reason why you moved those families and your own family that day? What was the main reason for doing that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The main reason for doing that was that you could feel danger in the air and that it seemed so nearby. We all panicked, all of us who were there, and we were taken by surprise, and we practically did not know where to go. We moved only 200 metres away, and it seemed safer for our families to move them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the civilians remain in these houses until the end, or, rather, during those three days?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: In that shelter by the house of Niko Vidovic, there were three or four Muslim families too. Our neighbours, Ramo Bilic's wife and children; then his brother Zijad Bilic with his wife; and also the family Strmonja, two brothers with their wives, I think, they were there. The next day, in the evening, there was some kind of panic. Someone had told them that a group of Mujahedeen had passed from the direction of Krtina Mahala, and they all escaped in the direction of Rovna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a moment, please. When you say they all escaped in the direction of Rovna, you are talking about all the people who were in those shelters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I say that, I'm referring to women, children, the elderly. I'm referring to all of those who were in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you realise that they had escaped to Rovna?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: In the evening, it was already getting dark, and there was a bit of drizzle, and I went to see where my family was and what this place was like, and I went there. There was a man over there, I can't even remember who he was, and there was no one else over there, and he said that a Mujahedeen unit had come from the direction of Krtina Mahala and that there was panic all over and they all escaped in the direction of Ronva. I was truly horrified. I was desperate. I didn't know a thing. I stood there. I went back to Ivo Kupreskic's house where we were all together again, and we commented about this. We had no information. It was difficult to explain. But I was in a terrible state then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just show us on the map where Rovna is, in which direction, and how far away is Rovna from Santici -- or, rather, Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Rovna is in this direction. This road leads to Rovna. It crosses the Lasva River. And then this part is the area of Rovna, that is to say, on the other side of the Lasva. That's about two kilometres approximately (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how the women, children, and elderly went there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know a thing. I found out only later, when I saw my wife and when I talked to her, but otherwise I did not know. She told me that they had left in a state of total panic, and that there was practically no organisation; everybody just grabbed their children and escaped. And she said that it was a really crazy panic and rush.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the next day they went to Rovna? Let us go back to the first day: Where did you spend the night? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I think that nobody slept during the first night. We spent all the time between the depression and our shelters, or rather where our families were. So practically all day we were on that -- in that area, between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the night?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The night too. Also at the edge of this depression, towards Ahmici. And from time to time we would come to Ivo Kupreskic's house, which was the first one at the edge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was happening on the second day? Did you stay where you were, and could you hear shooting still in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The second day, fire could constantly be heard. On the second day it moved deeper inside, in the direction of upper Ahmici. So it went deeper inside the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything change where you were? Did you go anywhere, did you stay where you -- in the depression?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: On the second day, practically I found out that my family were -- in the shelter where it had moved was the family of my neighbours, my Muslim neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which family was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: That was the family of Zijad Bilic, Ramo Bilic, and Strmonja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in the same shelter where your wife was?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were in the shelter in Niko Vidovic's house. My father told me that they were there, and that they were asking me to try -- because I was working for the international committee at that time. People there thought that they could do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the members of international organisations?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was all UNPROFOR to us. Humanitarian organisations, whoever, whatever organisations were there, we thought of them as UNPROFOR. So they told me they were there. They were afraid, and they asked me to try to call an acquaintance to try to get them, to take them out. So together with Zoran Kupreskic, I went there to see them. Zijad Bilic did not dare leave the basement, not even to go to the toilet. So my wife called me, and she told me that. So then I tried to give him some courage; I accompanied him to the bathroom. They were really terrified. After that, Zoran and I went to telephone. I called my secretary at that time, Ranka Gotovac, who spoke English -- I don't speak English -- and we asked -- I asked her to call the English unit of UNPROFOR, the Cheshire Regiment in Bila, to call them so that they would come and evacuate the Bilic family. They did not come. Zoran and I called Ranka several times, and Ranka called an acquaintance of ours, Edin Novalic, who was an interpreter in the Cheshire Regiment, in the engineering unit. They didn't come. They came at one point within 150 metres, an armoured vehicle came. I don't know whether it came to get them or it just came by chance, but an armoured vehicle did come on the second day to the shelter. But nobody actually came out of the vehicle; it just turned around and went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Bilics remained there, so the Bilic and the Strmonja family survived the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Their houses were not burned. They were among the few that were not burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, could we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Ms. Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at these photographs and tell us whether your house is depicted on the photographs, and whether the shelter is in your house.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D92/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, could you please tell us whether on the first two photographs your house is depicted?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, my house, and the house of my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The photograph number 5, does that show the basement room, and is that used as a shelter?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, photograph number 5 shows the basement room that was used as a shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at photograph number 3; is that the garage where Mirjan Santic was brought?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether you could put your questions in a different way, not as leading questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us what building is depicted in photograph number 3.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: This is the garage and the woodshed that belongs to me and my father, and this is where Mirjan Santic was brought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph number 1: Could you please tell us, in which direction does the road towards Udelina (phoen) go? Do you see from here where it leads?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph number 1, I can indicate the beginning. It's behind the garage. That's the start of the depression. The road -- you can't see the road, because it's much lower than this terrain here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph number 2: It's a close-up of the garage. Can you see the beginning of the road there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: That's this part here, behind the garage, so you can't see the very beginning, because it's lower. Photograph number 2 is obviously just a closer -- depicts more closely the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph number 4: Could you tell us what you see there? What side -- from what side of the house was this taken?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Photograph number 4 was taken from the front side of the house, and you can see the entrance to the basement, or the shelter, at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That side is the side where the entrance is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is where the entrance is, and it's turned towards the south. It's turned towards the house of Sulejman Ahmic, which is what I said at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the garage on photograph number 4?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: You can't see the garage on photograph number 4, because it's on the other side of the house, so it's covered by the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a roof here that you can see next to this blue car; what is that? Behind the blue car.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Behind the blue car, possibly you can see a part of the roof of a summer house. I don't know whose summer house it is. The man is from Zenica, but he's living and working in Germany. That's opposite the garage, and the road passes between the garage and the summer house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the fact that you can see that part which is very low indicate the fall of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The fall of the terrain can be seen here, behind the car is where the line stops, and then you can see the line of the forest. So the depression is here (Indicating), behind the car, behind the garage. The road goes in one direction, then it goes in the other direction here (Indicating), through this depression, towards the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court what happened on the third day.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The fire moved to this part, towards Pirici, on the third day, so I can show that on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: The firing shifted towards Pirici. And this forest was pretty large at that time; now it's been cut down. This is the part towards the upper part of the village, towards Pirici (Indicating). That's where the shooting was. Now the terrain looks completely different. From where we were there, it was a very thick, high forest, and you couldn't see anything. You couldn't even see the houses then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show on the photograph where the fire came from? Could you determine that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, you could hear it up there. And it was very deep inside Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear firing in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, you could hear shooting everywhere at the time. It's very difficult even now to specify where. There was fire everywhere, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. So what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: In the second half of the third day, all adult males from that area where we were, they directed us in the direction of Pirici. Some armed soldiers, in camouflage uniforms, two of them came to where we were, and they told us that we had to go towards Pirici and Barin Gaj. At the time, a lot of people were still arriving, and I recognised some from Vitez. They were not very well armed, and they were mostly dressed in civilian clothes. We were told to pass the Kupreskic houses and towards the summer houses, towards Pirici. We went together: Myself, Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Dragan Vidovic, Stipan, Dragance Vidovic, Pudja Miroslav, and there were a lot of other men. So we passed by the house of Zoran's neighbour, Enver, who was a baker. And that's where I saw for the first time a few dead people. Zoran I think had a nervous breakdown there. He started to shout and to cry; he couldn't control himself. It was pretty ugly to watch that, because one corpse was burned, and it was very difficult to look at that. We managed to calm him down. I think I was the one who really tried to calm him down. We passed up there by the houses of the closest neighbours, by Botic's summer house, and then we got to the upper part of the village of Pirici. We saw the uninhabited house of Gavro Vidovic. That night we spent the night there, and Slavko Papic came to see us. He's one of our neighbours. He told us that we need to dig trenches in order to fortify lines. So I remained there that night. We dug some trenches; we spent the night there. Then on the next day, at 9.00 in the morning, they came to get me from the defence office. Dragan Strbac came and told me that I should report to Vitez, because they needed a lot of engineers, construction engineers, people who can organise fortification, the digging of shelters, trenches, and so on. And then around 9.00 on the fourth day, I left the terrain of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The four days that you spent there, was any mobilisation carried out?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, if any mobilisation had been carried out, I would have taken part in it. I didn't notice, and I don't know that mobilisation was carried out. I personally was not a part of it. I'm not even on the ballot. I think for sure I can say that that day there was no mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody take down the names of the men who were brought to the lines? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Up until the 9.00 in the morning on the fourth day when I was there nobody had come, and after that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come back to Ahmici after that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: After that I was in Vitez. My organisation, the IRC -- the telephones were still working. They sent a fax to the municipal government, and they were requesting that I, as an engineer, should not serve my military duty, so I was released from service. On the 15th of May they organised the transportation for my wife and children, the IRC did that. Then on the 13th of May (sic) I went to the IRC office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then could you tell us whether you returned to Ahmici then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: After the war ended I never went back to Ahmici. I built a house in Vitez. I go to see my parents every now and then, but I do not intend to live there nor did I go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you go back to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: There are many reasons. It's spooky. I can't live there as a normal person. At least I think I'm a normal person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you think that you could have done something on that 16th? Could you have stopped the conflict? Could you have helped people more than you did, as you described it, that you tried to help the Bilics and the Strmonjas?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: On that day we just happened to be there by accident of birth, I should say. We could not choose where we were to be born. We happened to be there. We did not participate. We helped as much as we could. We helped the Bilics, and they were somehow within our midst, and they remained alive and their houses were not torched. We could not exercise any more influence, and I think that was accidental that their houses remained intact. I really think that we could not have influenced anything in any way. I mean, for things not to develop as they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also say whether during those three days, for as long as the conflict took, more or less intensively, were you separated from Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic and the Vidovics for a longer period of time, any longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Mirjan, Zoran and I practically did not separate at all. Dragance Vidovic, Stipan, Milutin Vidovic left immediately directly from that place towards his house, and later on the first day of the conflict he came to see us several times. So we were all running about and trying to collect information. During those first three days and the fourth day, until 9.00, I can confirm quite freely that I spent almost all the time with Mirjan, and Zoran, and Dragan Samija, and Pudza, Miroslav Vidovic, Dragan Stipan, my father was there every now and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your father?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: My father was in front of the shelter, in front of my house, and he had piled up some wood there, and he was there in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you also tell the court who Nenad Santic was?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Nenad Santic was an inhabitant of Santici, an acquaintance of mine. He actually lived in Donja Ronva. I knew him. He worked at the gasoline station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any special post in the village? Did he have any special importance?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. As far as I know, Nenad Santic was killed at Busovacke Staje as a rank-and-file soldier, and had he had any special post I would have known, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please just have a look at this document. Is this a document that pertains to you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D93/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a certificate of the International Rescue Committee, and it says that you are employed at the IRC, together with Ranka Gotovac, and basically they ask that the HVO government let you work for them. This is a document that was issued on the 4th of May, 1993, and at that time you had already left Vitez, is that correct, or were you still there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I was in Vitez till the 30th of May, because I had no opportunity of moving my family away so that I could go out and do the travel. And on the 15th of March, Todd Cleaver, who then worked at the IRC, took by car my wife and family to Split, and I left with an IRC convoy on the 30th of May with the consent of the HVO government. I went to Zenica and I was in Zenica until the 15th of July, when it became rather dangerous, and then from Zenica I left -- went to Split with a French convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person that is mentioned here together you with, Ranka Gotovac, is that the person that you called for the purpose of evacuating the Bilics?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that you worked for the IRC; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: After that I was the participant and organiser of Bijeli Put for Bosna Srebrna, a convoy. After that, on the 30th of April, 1994, I came to Vitez again. In Vitez an IRC office was opened for that part of Central Bosnia which was at that time under Croatian control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. I have completed my examination, and I would just like to tender into evidence exhibits from 85 -- 85/2 through 93/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not really an objection. I agree with the request. However, I would like, since some of the pages are extracts from a book and that those pages were given to the Tribunal, I would like that the entire book be placed within the case file of the Tribunal. This might be useful for ascertaining the truth, and it seems to me ideal that we move that way. If a translation problem were to arise, we could bring to the Trial Chamber the entire translation, in English, of the work.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Of course I agree, Mr. President, and of course I think that the entire book should be tendered. I didn't have this, but I see that the OTP does have that book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Right. So all these documents are admitted into evidence, and in addition, the whole book will be then provided by the -- in English and in the original Croatian by the OTP. Counsel Pavkovic, there is any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just like to ask something. Actually, earlier on in the part of the proceedings that was conducted by the Prosecutor, we tendered a document from the 16th of April, 1993, D16/2. This was a report of the military police which was signed for the Commander Pasko Ljubicic by some person who we did not manage to establish. At that time it was not tendered into evidence, this report, but I thought that certain facts had not been ascertained. However, the witness who was questioned at that time, Witness AA, confirmed that this stamp, which is at the bottom of the page, is the stamp of the command of the 4th Battalion of the military police. This was a protected witness, AA, and at that time he was an official of the military police. Since the witness today confirmed that the military police was in Ahmici, in view of the fact that from this admitted exhibit, which relates to the text of Pasko Ljubicic, it has also been established that the military police was in Ahmici, I would like to ask that this Defence Exhibit also be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This will be D16/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't believe that the witness identified today -- authenticated the signatory or the seal which is on the document. What he said about what he saw during that day in the village of Ahmici seems to be quite definite. It does not suffice to authenticate the document. I do not think that after this testimony today we can consider that this document has been sufficiently authenticated to be tendered as evidence, as I submit, to your judgment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, but can I just comment on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just want to say the following: The authenticity of this document has been corroborated, in fact, by the statement of Witness AA who was heard, I believe, in October last year. He confirmed that this stamp is the stamp of the military police of the 4th Battalion of the military police. Therefore, it was undeniable even then that that stamp is correct and that it comes from the 4th Battalion. What we did not know then is the substance, that the military police was in Ahmici at the time. However that witness also confirmed that Pasko Ljubicic was the commander, the stamp is undeniable, and also the substance is there. We can say that certain things have been authenticated. I believe that now we should admit this not only on the basis of the statement of this witness, but on the basis of the testimony and the substance of the testimony of Witness AA. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If you permit me, Mr. President, and I answer Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, the witness who testified before the Tribunal today, during the examination-in-chief, did not mention any specific military unit that was in Ahmici, he simply identified soldiers who -- that he was careful and hypothetical in his assertions that those people might have been members of the HVO military police. Therefore, he denied officially, and formally identified the unit to which those HVO soldiers belonged, nor the document in question. I'm not trying to prejudice what's going to happen in the future, but I can say that today is not appropriate, and the testimony that's just been heard by the Tribunal, is not the correct testimony to allow us to tender this document. Perhaps this might be possible at another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The Court finds the arguments put forward by the Prosecutor convincing, and so, therefore, we rule that the -- on the further occasion it will be possible to take into account this document and see whether it can be admitted into evidence, but not today, for the reasons, as I say, put forward by the Prosecutor. We can now move on to the issue of whether or not there is any cross-examination by other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to inform you that other Defence counsel do not intend to question this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before we then proceed to the cross-examination, let me say that the Court is somewhat mystified by what is now happening -- I should call it the strategy of the Defence, because I think the Defence has insisted throughout that they should first of all deal with Count 1 and then move on to other Counts, but, actually, the last two witnesses actually have dealt with Counts 2 through 11. So I wonder whether there's any particular reason. We would like to have some clarification from Defence counsel whether they intend to continue with Count 1, to exhaust Count 1, general Count on persecution, and then and only then move on to other Counts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, since these are our witnesses, we believe that Count 1 and the other Counts of the indictment are truly interrelated. We have now moved on to these witnesses that will be speaking about the other Counts as well, and we cannot separate them perfectly, and this will fully exhaust our defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But at the beginning you said that all Defence counsel would first of all deal with Count 1. So do you mean to say that you go on with Count 2 through 11, and then after other Defence counsel will go back to Count 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. President, we have all completed Count 1, except for the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic, and now we are in separate parts of the Defence case. I see that the lawyers for Vlatko Kupreskic have not presented witnesses dealing with Count 1 until now. So we will not be going to Count 1, and we are now in our separate part of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try and understand this position. From the list which we have, which was dated the 25th of January, there are, on the list, some seven or so witnesses, Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, who are apparently to be called on Count 1. Now, are we to understand then that you will not be calling those witnesses? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the time being that is our position. I think that we will not be calling other witnesses related to Count 1. For the time being we believe this is not necessary. However, the only thing that happened is that the Prosecutor presented some new documents, and perhaps we may need some new witnesses. This can be a general witness, but it depends on the direction in which the proceedings move, but for the time being we do not intend to call any other witnesses related to Count 1, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That means, if I understood you correctly, that means that you will now go on with the various Counts and other Defence counsel will start with other Counts after 11, so 12 and so on. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Except for the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic, Mr. President, because he has a separate list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel Krajina has -- yes, Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to say that the Defence of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, regarding Count 1 of the indictment, only has one expert, that's an expert witness, the Supreme Court president that we mentioned, and we will have no other witnesses for Count 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, regarding Count 1 for Drago Josipovic, the witnesses charge him directly for crimes of persecution which could relate to Count 1, but because they relate only to that accused, I think that only two witnesses will be brought to testify about that, regarding Count 1 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Then you will call those two witnesses when it is your turn to make your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes. There will not be a lot of witnesses for Drago Josipovic. It will be in continuity. It will be about nine witnesses altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Shall we then move to cross-examination? Cross-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sakic. My name is Franck Terrier, I'm one of the attorneys for the Prosecution, and as has surely been explained to you, I'm going to ask you a few questions further to your testimony. First of all, since you spoke about your family to us on several occasions, I would like you to clarify how many children you had in 1993, and how old they were.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: In 1993 I had the same as I have now. I had two children. My daughter, at that time, was six and a half years old, about six years and three months old, and my son is 17 months younger, so about four and half years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You lived in the house, pictures of which we saw, and you lived there with your parents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. The house has two entrances. I was living on the first floor and my mother and my father were living on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you always live in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I lived in that house. That house is in Pirici. This is about 150 metres away from Ahmici, and I lived there for the last 15 years perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony you spoke about your professional activities, and in particular your work obligation, which meant that you had to supply things to the HVO. Did I understood your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that you did understand my statement. I had no work duty towards the HVO. I don't even know if the HVO existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I did misunderstand something, and I can stand corrected, but I'm speaking about the time -- let me be clear -- the time from April -- or at least from the spring of 1992 to the beginning of 1993. I had thought that I had understood -- perhaps I was wrong -- that you had spoken about a work obligation, a service obligation, which you had to perform for the HVO during that period.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I said the following, and I will repeat that: I worked on Salvation Road. This is a road that was jointly financed by the municipality of Vitez, Busovaca, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Zenica, and we worked there for a salary, as a company. So I was in charge of a section of two and a half kilometres. So each town had their own team. I don't know how they financed it, but during that time we received our regular salary. I spent a couple of months on that road exclusively as a civil engineer, a person in charge of a part of a section of the road; in charge of the section that was the obligation of his municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, do you have any military experience?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I only have military experience from my military service in the Yugoslav People's Army in the period from 1979 to 1980. So the military experience of regular military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you had some weapons in your house, and you spoke about a hunting rifle, a revolver, and an automatic pistol; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. I had a Crvena Zastava revolver of 7,9 millimetres; I had a shotgun, which I had a permit for because I was a member of the Vitez hunting society. Then after the fall of Jajce, I bought an automatic rifle, a Kalashnikov. You understood me properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To talk about this automatic rifle,

utterances.speaker: MR. SAKIC
utterances.text: When did you buy it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when. I think I bought it five or six days after the fall of Jajce, at the time when Vitez was overwhelmed, overran with civilians who were retreating and who were offering everything that they had for sale in order to get money, but I can't really precisely remember when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whom did you buy the weapon from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. From some inhabitant of Jajce who was retreating. It was at that time just like buying cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean that everybody around you was buying weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that; I said that people who were retreating from Jajce were selling everything, including weapons, and I said that I bought a weapon for myself. Whether others were buying them or not, probably some people did and some didn't. In view of the danger, latent danger which was present, it was better for everybody to have weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was to defend yourself, defend your family, I'm sure, that you bought the weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I bought the weapons for self-protection, in order to feel better. I just thought I would feel better, safer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much did you pay for the weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I don't think I paid more than 300 German marks for it. 300, maybe 350 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your monthly salary at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: At that time, my -- there was no monthly salary, because I had stopped working at the municipal utilities office. So I had to fend for myself, practically. At that time, I didn't have any salary at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that 300 German marks, under conditions at that time, represented a relatively significant sum?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, for somebody, it probably did. Not for me, not at that time, and not now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that you had somewhat of a fortune; is that correct? You had some money, and that you still have some assets?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that 300 German marks is not a fortune, and you know yourself -- well, of course I had more than that at that time, and I have more than that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you buy ammunition at that same time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony, you mentioned these village patrols in which you participated. Could you tell us who organised them and who was in command, in Pirici, specifically, where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I think the village guards, after the first state fell apart, were organised spontaneously as a form of protection, and I wouldn't say that they were organised in any particular way. It was probably some kind of micro-organisation. There were four or five of us gathering around a house. There was no special structure; not as far as I know, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, would it be correct to say that if we don't speak about a command for these village patrols, would it be correct to speak, for instance, about coordination?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: If there had been any coordination, I would probably have had to take part in the village guards. But since this was a voluntary, self-organised thing, I took part maybe a couple of times, not more than that, so that there was no coordination to speak of at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you participated in that guard duty, were you armed with that Kalashnikov which you had acquired?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I took part only once. It was a walk; I wouldn't even call it a patrol. We walked along that road, myself and Miroslav Pudza, and of course -- I think I had a hunting rifle, I was carrying that, and I gave him the Kalashnikov. I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you know Slavko Papic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I know Slavko Papic. I've known him for at least 20 years. They moved to 300 or 400 metres away from my house. They've been there for the past ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't Slavko Papic responsible for things in the command or coordination or the organisation of these village guards?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I had no contacts with him, so I can't deny that or confirm that. I personally think that he did not. The first time I saw him, as I said earlier, was below Barin Gaj, in such a place, and it seemed logical to me at the time, since he was a reserve officer of the old Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that it was logical for him to exercise that kind of responsibility in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I said that it was logical, it seemed logical to me, for him -- at the location where we were, for him to give us suggestions on that third day of the conflict. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the HVO was formed at that time. I wouldn't say that I -- I had ever seen him in a uniform at all. I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be very clear, when you speak about October of 1992, at that period of October 1992, it seems that the HVO existed. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, you say "it seems." I can't say that it existed, because I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, you're telling us that you don't know whether in October 1992 the HVO existed? Have I understood your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I say that I don't know, I confirm that I don't -- I didn't know whether in October of '93 the HVO had been formed.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that we be perfectly clear here for the witness, let me look at the transcript: I'm speaking about October 1992. Therefore you're telling us that you don't know whether the HVO existed in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I confirm again -- I slipped; I'm saying that I did not know if in October of 1992 the HVO had been formed. I confirm again that I did not know whether this was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that things in this respect be very clear, when you say "the HVO," what are you referring to, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: When I say "the HVO," I mean the abbreviation, the Croatian Defence Council. The HVO, the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what did that Croatian Defence Council cover, in terms of organisation, in terms of staff, in terms of materiel, and function? What does all of that cover? What is the HVO, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Well, look, at the time I was working as a civil engineer. Then I stopped, and I started to work privately as a civil engineer. If I had any affinity to be there to find out, I would probably have been in the army. I was very interested in that work. I wanted to secure in that chaos a normal living for my family. So I really don't know anything about the structure. Absolutely, I'm not even in the records, I'm not even on the ballot lists, if you believe me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt what you're telling me.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: It's just a word that I use, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you begin to work for the humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: Officially I was accredited on the 15th of January, 1993; but in December of '92 I worked for them in the capacity of a contractor. The first job that I did for the IRC was a roof in Vitez which was blown off, so there were some children playing there. This was the first official job that I did for them. But I became an official employee of the IRC on the 15th of February of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could one think that at -- at that point we're working for a military organisation, an American one, that you had learned that there was such a thing as the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKIC
utterances.text: I don't speak English, and the people who were there, we communicated exclusively -- we talked exclusively about construction, civil engineering. I worked as a consultant. So I was really doing only my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to move to another area now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We can resume tomorrow.
